messages.content: I want to develop textual entailment models that generalize to unseen quantifier scope compositions while distinguishing semantic changes from paraphrases. What does that goal ask of the models?

It asks them to handle premise–hypothesis relationships involving combinations of quantifier scopes they have not previously encountered, without treating every change in wording as a change in meaning. They need to distinguish a meaning-preserving paraphrase from a scope change that alters whether the relationship is entailment, contradiction, or neutrality.
What does “unseen quantifier scope compositions” emphasize?

The emphasis is on generalization beyond familiar combinations of quantifiers and their relative scopes. Recognizing individual quantifier words is not enough: the model needs to respond to how their scopes interact in a composition it has not seen before.
Can you give a small conceptual illustration of why scope matters?

Compare “For every student, there is a book that the student read” with “There is a book that every student read.” The first allows different students to have read different books; the second requires a book shared across all the students. The wording is close, but the scope difference can matter to an entailment judgment.
So would any reversal of those scopes automatically be a contradiction?

No. A difference in meaning does not by itself establish contradiction. Whether a particular premise–hypothesis pair is entailing, contradictory, or neutral depends on what each sentence says and on the direction of the comparison. The target specifically concerns scope reversals that change the label, not a rule that every reversal must do so.
How does neutrality fit into this goal?

Neutrality remains one of the three relationships the model must distinguish, alongside entailment and contradiction. For instance, a premise might leave a hypothesis about a shared book unresolved rather than guarantee it or rule it out. The model should not turn an unresolved relationship into an entailment merely because the sentences use similar words.
And contradiction should not just mean that the two sentences look different?

Right. Contradiction is a semantic relationship, not a measure of surface difference. A change in phrasing may preserve meaning, and a scope change may alter meaning without making the two claims incompatible. The intended judgment has to follow the relationship between the meanings.
What is the quantitative target for the three-way judgments?

The requirement is at least 85% balanced accuracy on entailment, contradiction, and neutrality across unseen scope compositions. That is a performance target for the three-way task in that setting, not a claim that the models have already achieved it.
Does that sentence give a separate 85% minimum for each of the three labels?

It specifies at least 85% balanced accuracy across the three categories; it does not state three separate per-label minimums. The point of naming entailment, contradiction, and neutrality is that the target concerns the full three-way distinction.
There is also a requirement about paraphrases. How should I read it?

Predictions should be preserved across 95% of meaning-preserving paraphrases. If a paraphrase leaves the relevant meaning and inference relationship intact, the model should ordinarily give the same prediction rather than react to wording alone.
Is prediction preservation the same thing as getting those predictions right?

No. Consistently giving the same prediction across paraphrases measures stability, but the shared prediction could still be wrong. That is why the paraphrase-preservation requirement and the at-least-85% balanced-accuracy requirement express different aspects of the goal.
What qualifies as meaning-preserving here?

It means the reformulation keeps the meaning relevant to the premise–hypothesis relationship, including any scope distinctions that affect it. Calling a rewrite a paraphrase should not conceal a shift from, say, potentially different books for different students to one book shared by everyone.
How does the 90% figure differ from the 95% figure?

The model should preserve predictions across 95% of meaning-preserving paraphrases, but detect 90% of label-changing scope reversals. The first target concerns stability when the meaning stays the same; the second concerns sensitivity when reversing scope genuinely changes the inference label.
Does detecting a scope reversal mean changing the prediction whenever quantifier order changes?

Not indiscriminately. The stated 90% target is for label-changing scope reversals. A superficial change in order is not enough to establish that the label changed, so blanket prediction changes would miss the distinction the goal is meant to capture.
Could a paraphrase look quite different while preserving the prediction?

Yes. Surface similarity is not the criterion in the paraphrase requirement; preservation of the relevant meaning is. The model is supposed to remain stable even when the wording changes, provided the reformulation does not change the inference relationship.
Conversely, could two sentences look very similar but require different treatment?

Yes. Small changes to the ordering or scope of quantifiers can change what a sentence commits to. When that change also changes the label for a premise–hypothesis pair, it falls on the semantic-change side of the distinction rather than the meaning-preserving-paraphrase side.
Are the two percentages asking for the same sort of behavior on different examples?

They ask for complementary behaviors. The 95% requirement asks the model not to change its prediction when meaning is preserved; the 90% requirement asks it to detect reversals when the label changes. Neither behavior should be applied indiscriminately to the other kind of case.
How does that connect back to generalizing across unseen compositions?

On an unseen composition, the model still needs to attend to the semantic relationship rather than rely only on familiar wording. The at-least-85% balanced-accuracy target concerns its three-way judgments there, while the 95% and 90% targets test whether its responses remain appropriately stable or change for the right semantic reason.
Does this goal prescribe a particular training method or say the thresholds have been reached?
No. It states what the models are to achieve and the numerical criteria for assessing that goal. It does not specify an implementation method or report completed results.
Let me check my understanding: the model should ignore wording differences only when they preserve meaning, and notice scope differences when they actually change the label.

That captures the distinction. More precisely, the targets are at least 85% balanced accuracy across entailment, contradiction, and neutrality on unseen scope compositions; prediction preservation across 95% of meaning-preserving paraphrases; and detection of 90% of label-changing scope reversals.
What approach are you proposing for this goal?

The proposal is to train ScopeGraph-NLI with three complementary elements: compositional scope-graph supervision, a paraphrase-consistency loss, and label-aware contrastive training on scope reversals. Together, they are intended to help the model attend to quantifier scope, stay stable under meaning-preserving rewrites, and respond when a scope reversal changes the entailment label.
What does compositional scope-graph supervision contribute?

It would provide a training signal about how the relevant scope relationships are composed, rather than leaving the model to infer everything from surface wording alone. The intended connection is that understanding those relationships could help ScopeGraph-NLI handle quantifier scope compositions it has not seen before. The proposal does not specify a particular graph representation or how the supervision would be obtained.
Is the scope graph meant to replace the entailment judgment?

No. The proposed supervision concerns the structure of scope, while the task remains judging the relationship between a premise and a hypothesis. Scope structure can matter to that judgment, but identifying a scope relationship is not itself the same as assigning entailment, contradiction, or neutrality.
Why call the supervision compositional?

The emphasis is on relationships among scopes as they combine, not just on recognizing individual quantifiers in isolation. That matches the aim of generalizing to unseen scope compositions. It is a description of what the supervision is intended to emphasize, not a claim that the resulting generalization has already been demonstrated.
What role does the paraphrase-consistency loss play?

It is intended to discourage ScopeGraph-NLI from changing its prediction merely because an input has been reworded without changing its meaning. That addresses the stability side of the goal: a genuine paraphrase should not be mistaken for a semantic change.
Would that loss make the model give the same answer to every similarly worded sentence?

It should not be read that way. Paraphrase consistency applies when the relevant meaning is preserved, not whenever wording overlaps. Two sentences can be very similar in wording yet differ in quantifier scope, so the proposal also includes a signal aimed at recognizing consequential scope reversals.
Then what does the label-aware part of the contrastive training mean?

Conceptually, it means the treatment of a scope reversal should take the entailment label into account. The contrast is meant to help distinguish reversals that change the label from cases that should retain the same judgment. The proposal names label-aware contrastive training but does not prescribe a particular contrastive objective or pairing procedure.
Does it assume every reversal changes a label?

No. Reversing scope can change meaning without necessarily making every premise–hypothesis comparison switch labels. Being label-aware is important precisely because the training should not treat the presence of a reversal, by itself, as proof of a particular label change.
How can paraphrase consistency and contrastive training coexist without pulling in opposite directions?

They address different relationships. Paraphrase consistency is intended to keep predictions aligned when meaning is preserved; label-aware contrastive training on scope reversals is intended to make the model sensitive when a reversal changes the inference relationship. The proposal relies on maintaining that distinction rather than treating all rewrites alike.
Could a paraphrase change the wording around quantifiers and still fall under consistency?

Yes, if it preserves the scope relationships and the meaning relevant to the entailment judgment. The consistency signal is about meaning preservation, not about keeping particular words or a particular sentence shape fixed.
And if a rewrite changes the scope relationship?

Then it cannot simply be assumed to qualify for meaning-preserving consistency. Its effect on the premise–hypothesis label matters. The proposed label-aware contrastive component is directed at scope reversals, particularly the need to recognize those that change the label.
What is the division of labor among the three elements?

Compositional scope-graph supervision focuses on representing how scopes relate and combine. Paraphrase-consistency loss focuses on prediction stability under meaning-preserving wording changes. Label-aware contrastive training on scope reversals focuses on sensitivity to changes that affect the entailment label. Those are intended roles, not separate claims of measured effectiveness.
Would using only the scope-graph supervision settle the paraphrase issue?

The proposal does not make that claim. Scope-graph supervision addresses compositional scope information, while the paraphrase-consistency loss explicitly addresses stability under meaning-preserving reformulations. Including both expresses the intention to handle structure and invariance together.
Would the paraphrase-consistency loss alone tell the model what to do with a label-changing reversal?

Not by its stated purpose. A consistency signal is aimed at cases that should retain a prediction; it does not by itself express the desired response when a scope reversal changes the label. That is the distinct role of the label-aware contrastive component in this proposal.
Are the training examples, graph construction, and exact losses already specified?

No. The proposal specifies ScopeGraph-NLI and the three training elements, but it does not give a dataset, a graph-construction procedure, loss equations, or implementation details. Those should not be inferred from the names of the components.
So this is an approach to the goal, not a report of a trained model?
Exactly. It proposes training ScopeGraph-NLI in this way. It does not say training has occurred, report predictions, or establish that any performance target has been reached.
What should I keep in mind when describing why these components belong together?

Describe them as complementary proposed signals for separating semantic structure from wording: scope-graph supervision for compositional scope relationships, paraphrase consistency for meaning-preserving rewrites, and label-aware contrastive training for consequential scope reversals. The connection to better generalization is the motivation for the proposal, not an observed outcome.
Can ScopeGraph-NLI handle held-out three-quantifier scope permutations while preserving passive paraphrases and detecting label-changing reversals?

That is an open question about ScopeGraph-NLI, not an established result. It asks whether the model can make appropriate entailment judgments for three-quantifier scope arrangements it has not encountered, keep its predictions stable when an active sentence is recast as a meaning-preserving passive, and recognize reversals that change the inference label.
What is distinctive about specifying three quantifiers?

With three quantifiers, the question concerns how several scope relationships work together. It is not just whether the model recognizes a single quantifier or notices that two quantifiers have exchanged places. A correct judgment has to reflect the meaning of the whole scope arrangement.
Does “held-out” mean the model has never seen any of the quantifier words?

Not necessarily. Here it describes held-out three-quantifier scope permutations. It does not, by itself, say that the individual quantifier words, sentence forms, or other features are entirely unfamiliar. The question is whether the model handles the unseen arrangements.
Is recognizing the scope arrangement enough to answer the question?

No. The model must use the arrangement to make an appropriate judgment about the premise–hypothesis relationship. It might identify a structural difference without drawing the right entailment conclusion, so handling a permutation involves more than merely noticing that the scopes differ.
How should I understand the passive-paraphrase part?

It asks whether a change from active to passive wording leaves ScopeGraph-NLI’s prediction intact when that change preserves the relevant meaning. Passive wording may change which phrase appears first or occupies the grammatical subject position without changing the intended inference relationship.
Does every active-to-passive rewrite count as a meaning-preserving paraphrase in a quantifier-scope question?

No. For this question, the important cases are passive paraphrases that actually preserve meaning, including the relevant scope interpretation. A passive rewrite should not be assumed to preserve meaning merely because it describes a similar event with reordered words.
Why might passive wording be a useful thing to ask about here?

It makes the distinction between grammatical form and semantic scope especially clear. If the meaning stays the same, the prediction should not change just because the sentence has become passive. At the same time, the model must remain responsive to scope differences that do change the inference relationship.
So preserving a prediction across a passive paraphrase is not the same as handling a held-out permutation?

Correct. The first asks for stability when a different expression has the same relevant meaning. The second asks whether the model can reason appropriately about a scope arrangement it has not seen. The question asks whether ScopeGraph-NLI can do both, rather than treating one as evidence that automatically establishes the other.
What counts as a label-changing reversal?

It is a reversal of scope that changes the correct inference label for the premise–hypothesis comparison. Detecting it means responding to that consequential semantic difference, not simply registering that the quantifiers have been rearranged.
Would a model pass that part by changing its prediction after every scope reversal?
No. The wording is specifically “label-changing reversals.” A rule that changes the prediction for every reversal would not distinguish cases where the label changes from cases where it does not.
Could a reversal change the sentence’s meaning but leave the inference label unchanged?

Yes. Meaning and an inference label are related but not identical: two different meanings can have the same relationship to a particular other sentence. That is why this question singles out reversals that change the label, rather than equating every semantic difference with a label change.
If ScopeGraph-NLI gives the same answer for a passive paraphrase, does that show it understood the paraphrase?

Not on its own. Stable predictions are compatible with understanding, but the same prediction could also be consistently mistaken. The question concerns preservation of predictions alongside appropriate handling of the underlying entailment relationship.
And if its answer changes for a scope reversal, is that automatically evidence of detecting the right change?

Not automatically. The relevant issue is whether the change tracks a reversal that changes the correct label and whether the resulting judgment reflects that label. A change in prediction merely because wording changed would not settle the question.
Does the question specify a particular collection of passive sentences or scope permutations?

No. It identifies the phenomena of interest—held-out three-quantifier scope permutations, passive paraphrases, and label-changing reversals—but gives no specific examples, collection, or results. We can clarify what the question asks without assuming how any particular evaluation is assembled.
Can the proposed training approach answer this question by itself?

The approach gives a reason to investigate the question, but a training proposal does not establish the answer. Whether ScopeGraph-NLI actually handles those held-out permutations while showing the two requested behaviors remains to be determined.
What would a positive answer have to encompass, conceptually?

It would have to encompass all three parts together: appropriate inference judgments for held-out three-quantifier scope permutations, stable predictions for genuinely meaning-preserving passive paraphrases, and sensitivity to scope reversals that change the correct label. Success on only one part would leave the rest of the question unanswered.
Could those parts come apart for the same model?

Conceptually, yes. A model might be stable under passive rewording yet fail to distinguish consequential scope changes, or react to scope changes yet be distracted by passive wording. That possibility is why the question puts the behaviors side by side rather than treating them as interchangeable.
Then the word “while” matters: it is asking for generalization without losing paraphrase stability or reversal sensitivity?

Exactly. “While” ties the requirements together. The question is not merely whether ScopeGraph-NLI handles an unseen three-quantifier arrangement in isolation; it also asks whether its judgments remain stable where passive wording preserves meaning and change appropriately where a scope reversal changes the label.

I want to state a hypothesis about ScopeGraph-NLI: it will reach 85% three-class balanced accuracy on held-out three-quantifier permutations, 95% passive-paraphrase agreement, and 90% scope-reversal detection. Is that a fair way to express it?

Yes, as a hypothesis. Those are predicted outcomes for ScopeGraph-NLI, not results that have been observed. The three figures address different parts of the question: three-class inference performance on held-out three-quantifier permutations, agreement across passive paraphrases, and detection of consequential scope reversals.
What exactly does the 85% figure refer to?

It refers to three-class balanced accuracy on held-out three-quantifier permutations. The three classes are entailment, contradiction, and neutrality. The hypothesis says ScopeGraph-NLI will reach 85% on that measure in that held-out setting.
Why specify balanced accuracy rather than just say accuracy?

Balanced accuracy makes the claim about performance across the classes, rather than describing only an undifferentiated share of correct answers. The hypothesis is specifically about the three-class judgment, so replacing “three-class balanced accuracy” with plain “accuracy” would make the stated prediction less precise.
Does that mean 85% for each class separately?
No. The hypothesis gives an 85% three-class balanced-accuracy figure; it does not state a separate 85% result for entailment, another for contradiction, and another for neutrality.
Does “held-out three-quantifier permutations” mean the prediction covers every possible kind of unfamiliar language?

No. It identifies the setting of the prediction: held-out permutations involving three quantifiers. It does not claim unrestricted generalization to every unfamiliar wording, construction, or inference problem.
How should I read the 95% passive-paraphrase agreement figure?

The hypothesis predicts 95% agreement in ScopeGraph-NLI’s predictions across passive paraphrases. In the context of the question, these are passive reformulations that preserve the relevant meaning. Agreement means the prediction remains the same across such a paraphrase; the figure should not be silently changed into a claim of 95% accuracy.
So matching answers across a paraphrase pair could still be wrong?

Yes. Agreement describes consistency between predictions, not whether the shared prediction is correct. That is why the 95% passive-paraphrase agreement prediction is distinct from the 85% three-class balanced-accuracy prediction.
Would a passive rewrite that changes the relevant scope meaning belong in that agreement claim?

Not simply because it is passive. The paraphrase part concerns meaning-preserving passive reformulations. If a rewrite changes the relevant meaning, requiring the same prediction would confuse paraphrase stability with insensitivity to a semantic change.
What is the 90% scope-reversal detection prediction saying?

It predicts that ScopeGraph-NLI will detect 90% of the scope reversals at issue in the question: reversals that change the inference label. It is about responsiveness to a consequential scope change, not about changing the prediction whenever quantifiers appear in a different order.
Is detection here interchangeable with three-class balanced accuracy?

No. The 85% figure concerns the model’s three-class judgments across held-out three-quantifier permutations. The 90% figure singles out its response to label-changing scope reversals. They focus on different aspects of the proposed performance, even though both concern inference labels.
And agreement and detection are deliberately pulling in different directions?

They call for different behavior in different semantic circumstances. For a meaning-preserving passive paraphrase, the prediction should agree; for a scope reversal that changes the label, the model should detect the difference. The hypothesis is that ScopeGraph-NLI can exhibit both behaviors, rather than applying a blanket rule to keep or change predictions.
Could I summarize the hypothesis as ‘ScopeGraph-NLI will get about 90% on quantifier tasks’?

That would blur three distinct predictions and change their numerical values. The stated hypothesis is 85% three-class balanced accuracy on held-out three-quantifier permutations, 95% passive-paraphrase agreement, and 90% scope-reversal detection. None of those is a general “about 90% on quantifier tasks” claim.
Does the hypothesis say why ScopeGraph-NLI would achieve those numbers?

It states predicted outcomes, not an explanation establishing that they will occur. The proposed training approach gives context for why one might examine these behaviors, but the hypothesis itself does not demonstrate a cause or provide evidence that the numbers have been reached.
If I discuss it in the future tense, am I making it sound too certain?

The future tense reflects the hypothesis’s wording—ScopeGraph-NLI *will reach* those figures—but it should remain clearly framed as a prediction. Saying “the hypothesis is that it will reach” preserves that distinction; saying “it reached” would turn a prediction into an unsupported result.
Is it important to keep the three conditions attached to their respective percentages?

Yes. The 85% figure belongs to three-class balanced accuracy on held-out three-quantifier permutations; 95% belongs to passive-paraphrase agreement; and 90% belongs to scope-reversal detection. Moving a percentage to a different condition would change the hypothesis.
So the full claim is not that any one of these numbers alone answers the question?

Right. The hypothesis predicts all three outcomes for ScopeGraph-NLI together: performance on held-out three-quantifier permutations, stability under meaning-preserving passive paraphrases, and detection of label-changing scope reversals. Each percentage describes its own aspect of that prediction.
How would we check the ScopeGraph-NLI hypothesis?

The plan is to construct ScopeSplit-3 with held-out scope permutations, train ScopeGraph-NLI, and then measure balanced accuracy, passive-paraphrase agreement, and scope-reversal detection. Those measurements would address the inference, paraphrase-stability, and reversal-sensitivity parts of the question.
What is ScopeSplit-3 in this plan?

ScopeSplit-3 is the named resource to be constructed with held-out scope permutations. In the context of the question, those are the three-quantifier permutations whose handling we want to examine. The plan does not specify the resource’s size, sentence templates, or construction procedure.
Why include held-out permutations rather than only examples with familiar scope arrangements?

The question asks whether ScopeGraph-NLI can handle scope permutations it has not encountered. Holding out permutations makes that generalization issue part of what is measured, rather than evaluating only familiar arrangements.
Does the plan say exactly which permutations will be held out?
No. It calls for ScopeSplit-3 to have held-out scope permutations but does not identify particular permutations or give a rule for selecting them.
Does “held-out” mean every word in those examples must also be unfamiliar?
No such condition is stated. The specified distinction concerns scope permutations; the plan does not say that quantifier words or all other aspects of the sentences must be novel.
What comes after constructing ScopeSplit-3?
The next stated step is to train ScopeGraph-NLI. After that, the plan calls for measuring the three named outcomes. It does not report that construction or training has already happened.
Does this plan give the training settings for ScopeGraph-NLI?
No. It identifies the model to train and the order of the work, but does not specify training settings or add an implementation procedure.
When you say “then measure,” what is being kept separate from training?

The plan treats measurement as a subsequent step rather than assuming training itself establishes how well the model performs. Training ScopeGraph-NLI would not, on its own, tell us its balanced accuracy, its agreement across passive paraphrases, or its detection of scope reversals.
What would the balanced-accuracy measurement tell us?

It would assess the model’s three-class judgments—entailment, contradiction, and neutrality—in the held-out scope-permutation setting. That addresses whether it can make appropriate inference distinctions when the scope composition is unfamiliar.
Would that single measurement answer the entire question?

No. Balanced accuracy addresses the three-class inference judgments, but the plan separately measures whether predictions agree across passive paraphrases and whether the model detects consequential scope reversals. Those behaviors should not be inferred solely from one accuracy figure.
What does measuring passive-paraphrase agreement add?
It examines prediction stability when passive wording preserves the relevant meaning. The concern is that a change in grammatical form should not, by itself, change the model’s inference judgment.
Could a high agreement measurement just mean the model repeats the same wrong answer?

It could. Agreement measures whether predictions match across the paraphrases, not whether those predictions are correct. That is one reason to keep passive-paraphrase agreement distinct from balanced accuracy.
Does the plan specify how passive paraphrases will be produced?

No. It calls for measuring passive-paraphrase agreement but does not specify how the paraphrases are produced or checked. The intended comparison is with passive reformulations that preserve the meaning relevant to the inference judgment.
And what is the scope-reversal measurement meant to show?

It is meant to show whether ScopeGraph-NLI detects scope reversals that change the inference label. That complements paraphrase agreement: the model should be stable where meaning is preserved but responsive where a reversal changes the judgment.
Would detecting every change in quantifier order count?

Not necessarily. The question concerns label-changing reversals, not every alteration in word order or scope. Measuring detection should retain that distinction; otherwise, a model could appear responsive simply by changing its prediction whenever the wording changes.
Does the plan define a precise scoring rule for scope-reversal detection?
No. It names scope-reversal detection as a measurement but does not give a scoring formula or a procedure for identifying the relevant reversals. Those details are not settled by this plan’s wording.
So ScopeSplit-3 is constructed first, but the plan does not spell out every example needed for each measurement?

Correct. The stated sequence is to construct ScopeSplit-3 with held-out scope permutations, train ScopeGraph-NLI, and then measure the three outcomes. It does not specify the complete contents of ScopeSplit-3 or exactly how the passive-paraphrase and scope-reversal comparisons will be assembled.
How do the measurements relate back to the question about handling the held-out permutations while preserving paraphrases and detecting reversals?

Each measurement addresses a different part of it. Balanced accuracy concerns inference judgments on the held-out scope permutations. Passive-paraphrase agreement concerns stability under meaning-preserving passive wording. Scope-reversal detection concerns sensitivity when a scope reversal changes the label. Considering them together is more informative for that question than treating any one as a substitute for the others.
Can we say the plan has already answered the question if all three measurements are listed?

No. Listing the measurements establishes what the plan proposes to examine, not what their values will be. The question remains open until the planned construction, training, and measurement have been carried out.

Then the careful wording is that we will construct ScopeSplit-3 with held-out scope permutations, train ScopeGraph-NLI, and afterward measure balanced accuracy, passive-paraphrase agreement, and scope-reversal detection?
Yes. That preserves both the stated order and the prospective status of the plan without adding unprovided details or presenting the intended measurements as results.
What are the concrete training and scoring quantities for this activity?

The specified activity is to train ScopeGraph-NLI on 24,000 ScopeSplit-3 examples, then score 3,000 held-out permutations, 1,000 passive paraphrases, and 1,000 label-changing reversals. Those are the quantities for the training and scoring portions; they are not reported performance results.
Is the 24,000 figure the number of examples used to train ScopeGraph-NLI?
Yes. It refers to 24,000 ScopeSplit-3 examples for training ScopeGraph-NLI. The activity does not give a finer breakdown of those training examples.
And the 3,000 figure is for examples encountered during training?

No. The 3,000 are specified as held-out permutations to score. The distinction matters because the activity is examining performance on scope permutations held out from training, rather than just scoring the 24,000 training examples.
Are the 3,000 held-out permutations the part used for the three-class balanced-accuracy measurement?

That is how this scoring activity connects to the stated measurement: judgments on held-out permutations bear on three-class balanced accuracy for entailment, contradiction, and neutrality. The activity gives the count of permutations to score, but it does not give an accuracy value.
Why score passive paraphrases separately?

Scoring 1,000 passive paraphrases addresses whether predictions remain consistent when passive wording preserves the relevant meaning. That is a different question from whether the model assigns the right three-way label on a held-out scope permutation.
Does “1,000 passive paraphrases” tell us whether that means 1,000 individual sentences or 1,000 paraphrase pairs?

No. The activity says to score 1,000 passive paraphrases, but it does not specify the counting convention or how they are paired for an agreement calculation. It would be premature to supply that detail.
What is special about the 1,000 scope reversals?

They are specified as 1,000 label-changing reversals. Scoring them addresses whether ScopeGraph-NLI detects a scope change that changes the correct inference label, rather than simply reacting to any change in quantifier order.
Would the count include reversals that alter the sentence’s meaning but leave the inference label unchanged?

The stated count is for label-changing reversals, so it should not be described as a count of all meaning-changing reversals. The activity does not say whether other kinds of reversals are also present elsewhere.
Can I add the three scoring counts and call them 5,000 distinct evaluation examples?

The three stated counts sum to 5,000 scoring instances, but the activity does not say whether the groups are mutually exclusive or how their units are counted. Calling them 5,000 *distinct* evaluation examples would add a condition that has not been specified.
Does the activity specify how ScopeSplit-3 is divided beyond those counts?
No. It specifies 24,000 ScopeSplit-3 examples for training and the three quantities to score. It does not provide a complete split design or explain how the scoring groups relate to one another.
Are the 1,000 passive paraphrases necessarily drawn from the 3,000 held-out permutations?

That relationship is not stated. We can say both groups are to be scored, but we cannot infer whether the passive paraphrases are drawn from the held-out permutations, overlap with them, or form a separate group.
Does specifying these sample sizes mean ScopeGraph-NLI has met any of the predicted percentages?

No. The activity specifies what to train on and what to score; it gives no measured balanced accuracy, passive-paraphrase agreement, or scope-reversal detection rate. Sample counts alone do not establish whether any predicted percentage is reached.
Should we describe the scoring as looking at three complementary behaviors?

Yes. The 3,000 held-out permutations concern inference judgments on unfamiliar scope arrangements; the 1,000 passive paraphrases concern prediction stability under meaning-preserving wording changes; and the 1,000 label-changing reversals concern sensitivity to consequential scope changes. The activity assigns a concrete scoring count to each behavior without reporting its outcome.
What is the most precise one-sentence description of the activity?

Train ScopeGraph-NLI on 24,000 ScopeSplit-3 examples and score 3,000 held-out permutations, 1,000 passive paraphrases, and 1,000 label-changing reversals, without treating those scoring counts as performance results.
What did ScopeGraph-NLI achieve on the three measurements?

ScopeGraph-NLI achieved 86.7% balanced accuracy on held-out permutations, 96.1% passive-paraphrase agreement, and 91.4% detection of label-changing scope reversals. These are reported measurements, each attached to a different behavior.
What does the 86.7% figure describe?

It is the balanced accuracy on held-out permutations. In this textual entailment setting, the judgments concern entailment, contradiction, and neutrality. The figure describes performance across those judgments on the held-out scope arrangements; it is not a passive-paraphrase agreement rate.
Does 86.7% mean the model got exactly that percentage right for each individual label?

No. Balanced accuracy summarizes performance across the classes. This result does not give separate figures for entailment, contradiction, and neutrality, so we should not assign 86.7% to each class individually.
What can we say specifically about passive paraphrases?

The reported passive-paraphrase agreement is 96.1%. That measures how consistently ScopeGraph-NLI’s predictions agree across the relevant passive paraphrases. It should not be redescribed as 96.1% balanced accuracy or as a separate claim that every agreeing prediction is correct.
Why does agreement leave room for error?

Two predictions can agree with each other while both being mistaken about the inference relationship. The 96.1% figure reports consistency across passive paraphrases; correctness across held-out permutations is represented by a different measurement.
And how should I interpret the 91.4% figure?

ScopeGraph-NLI detected 91.4% of label-changing scope reversals. The qualifier matters: the result concerns reversals that change the correct inference label, not a claim about detecting every possible scope difference or changing predictions whenever quantifiers move.
Does detecting a reversal just mean noticing that the wording changed?
No. The reported measure is label-changing scope-reversal detection. A wording change alone is not the semantic distinction at issue; the relevant reversal changes the inference label.
The three percentages are close to each other. Can we treat them as three estimates of one overall accuracy?

No. They measure different things: 86.7% balanced accuracy on held-out permutations, 96.1% passive-paraphrase agreement, and 91.4% label-changing scope-reversal detection. Combining them into a single accuracy figure would obscure those different conditions and measures.

Entailment concerns whether the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another; contradiction and neutrality concern different relationships between their meanings. The proposal does not say that checking a particular collection of finite models settles every possible inference.

Six-split reversal detection rose from 90.7% to 94.0%. The masked condition also exceeded the 93.1% no-contrast baseline.
How large was the increase from 90.7% to 94.0%?
It was 3.3 percentage points. That is the difference between the two reversal-detection rates, not a relative increase of 3.3%.
And how far above the no-contrast baseline was the masked result?
The masked result was 0.9 percentage points above the 93.1% no-contrast baseline: 94.0% minus 93.1%.
Which value belongs to which condition?

The comparison reports 90.7% before masking overlapping scope-forest negatives and 94.0% after masking them. The separate no-contrast baseline is 93.1%. All three figures concern six-split reversal detection.
Does 94.0% describe the no-contrast condition?
No. It is the result after masking the overlapping scope-forest negatives. The no-contrast baseline is 93.1%.
What does ‘overlapping’ mean in the masking condition?

The negatives targeted for masking share an oracle scope reading. Their scope forests can overlap in that reading even if they are not identical overall. The reported result does not say how many negatives were masked.
Were all ambiguous negatives masked?
That is not stated. The intervention is described as masking overlapping scope-forest negatives, not masking every ambiguous negative.
Does this result show that overlap was relevant to the reversal-detection difference?

It supports that interpretation: reversal detection was higher after the overlap-masking intervention, and the masked result exceeded the no-contrast baseline. The aggregate rates do not show which individual overlaps affected predictions or establish that overlap explains every error.
Does it prove that mislabeled negatives played no role?
No. This result measures what happened when overlapping negatives were masked. It does not, by itself, prove that every label was correct or rule out other contributors to reversal-detection errors.
What can we say about the prediction that masking would exceed 93.1%?

The reported 94.0% six-split reversal detection is strictly above 93.1%, so the numerical prediction for the masked condition is met. That observation does not turn every part of the proposed explanation for contrastive collisions into a proven mechanism.
Would a score of exactly 93.1% have exceeded the baseline?
No. Exactly 93.1% would have matched it. The reported 94.0% exceeds it by 0.9 percentage points.
Is the 3.3-point increase measured against the no-contrast baseline?
No. The 3.3-percentage-point increase is from 90.7% to 94.0% in the before-and-after masking comparison. The difference between 94.0% and the 93.1% no-contrast baseline is 0.9 percentage points.
Is this a balanced-accuracy result too?
No. The reported values are for six-split reversal detection. This finding does not give balanced accuracy for the masked condition.
Does it report passive agreement after masking?
No. Passive agreement is not reported in this finding, so we cannot say whether it rose, fell, or stayed the same.
Does six-split mean six random seeds were averaged?
Not necessarily. The stated unit is six splits, not six seeds. The finding does not specify a seed count or give a result for each split.
Can we tell whether masking helped on every split?
No. The finding reports six-split rates but no split-by-split breakdown. The aggregate increase does not establish that each split improved.
Can we calculate statistical significance from the three percentages?
No. The result gives no uncertainty estimate, example-level outcomes, or per-split values from which to assess statistical significance.
Does 94.0% mean every label-changing reversal was detected?
No. It is a 94.0% detection rate in this six-split evaluation, not perfect detection or a claim about every possible scope reversal.
Should a model change its prediction for every pair of overlapping forests?

No such rule follows. Overlapping forests share a possible scope reading, but may also contain distinct readings. The masking result concerns how negatives with overlap were handled during the intervention; it does not imply a universal prediction rule for overlapping forests.
Does the result tell us whether the model now distinguishes every paraphrase from every semantic change?
No. It reports an improvement in six-split reversal detection. It supplies no comprehensive paraphrase result or guarantee about every semantic distinction.
How should I summarize the finding without overstating its explanation?

Masking overlapping scope-forest negatives raised six-split reversal detection from 90.7% to 94.0%, which is 0.9 percentage points above the 93.1% no-contrast baseline. The measured improvement supports investigating overlap as a contributor, without establishing it as the sole cause of contrastive errors.
Which approach are we adopting for reversal contrast?
Adopt overlap-masked reversal contrast. The stated reason is its six-split reversal detection: it rises from 90.7% to 94.0%, outperforming contrast removal at 93.1% and relabeling at 91.0%.
What exactly is being masked?

The overlap in the reversal contrast: negatives whose scope forests share an oracle scope reading are masked. The decision adopts that overlap-masked approach; it does not specify a new masking algorithm or say that every ambiguous negative is removed.
Does adopting it mean removing reversal contrast altogether?
No. The decision retains reversal contrast with overlap masking. Contrast removal is a comparison condition, with 93.1% reversal detection, not the approach being adopted.
Can you keep the three comparison conditions straight for me?

With the overlap-masked reversal contrast, detection is 94.0%. With contrast removed, it is 93.1%. With relabeling, it is 91.0%. The decision also specifies that masking raises detection from 90.7% to 94.0%.
Which number is the starting point for the reported increase?

The starting reversal-detection figure is 90.7%, and the overlap-masked figure is 94.0%. Contrast removal’s 93.1% and relabeling’s 91.0% are separate comparisons, not the starting value in the 90.7%→94.0% increase.
How much of an increase is 90.7% to 94.0%?
It is an increase of 3.3 percentage points in reversal detection. That is a difference between percentages, not a relative increase of 3.3%.
How far ahead is overlap masking compared with removing contrast?
Its 94.0% reversal detection is 0.9 percentage points higher than the 93.1% for contrast removal.
And compared with relabeling?
The overlap-masked result of 94.0% is 3.0 percentage points higher than the 91.0% relabeling result, on the reversal-detection figures stated in the decision.
Does relabeling at 91.0% mean 91.0% of negatives had their labels corrected?
No. The 91.0% figure is reversal detection for the relabeling comparison, not a percentage of negatives relabeled. The decision compares detection rates across approaches.
Could I just say masking is better than both alternatives on every metric?

No. The decision says overlap-masked reversal contrast outperforms contrast removal and relabeling on reversal detection, using 94.0%, 93.1%, and 91.0%. It does not state a comparison on balanced accuracy or passive agreement.
Is the 94.0% result an entailment accuracy figure?
No. It is a reversal-detection rate. Calling it balanced accuracy or overall entailment accuracy would attach the number to a different measure.
Should I say the masked approach has reached 94.0% on every held-out permutation?
No. The decision uses the 94.0% six-split reversal-detection result. It does not give a separate detection rate for every split or say all individual held-out permutations scored 94.0%.
What does the comparison say about simply correcting labels?

For the reversal-detection comparison stated here, relabeling reaches 91.0%, while overlap-masked reversal contrast reaches 94.0%. The decision therefore adopts masking rather than choosing relabeling as the approach on the basis of these detection figures. It does not imply that no individual label ever needs correction.
Is the fact that masking beats removing contrast enough to explain why it works?

It establishes the reported performance comparison, not a complete causal explanation. The decision chooses overlap-masked reversal contrast because its detection rate is higher under these stated conditions; it does not say every reversal-detection error was due to overlap.
Does the decision tell us to discard paraphrase alignment or oracle-forest distillation?
No. It makes a decision about reversal contrast and its masking. It does not state a change to paraphrase alignment or oracle-forest distillation.
What if two scope forests share a reading but also differ in another reading? Does masking declare them identical?

No. Sharing a reading does not mean their entire forests are identical. The decision adopts masking of overlapping reversal negatives; it does not declare the remaining scope readings equivalent or prescribe one inference label for every pair of overlapping forests.
And does adopting contrast imply every scope reversal should change the predicted label?

No. A reversal does not automatically change the inference label. Overlap-masked reversal contrast is chosen for its reported detection of relevant reversals, not as a rule to flip a prediction whenever quantifier scopes differ.
Does this decision claim the approach will outperform those comparisons on any future benchmark?

No. Its comparison is the stated six-split reversal-detection result: 94.0% with overlap masking, versus 93.1% without contrast and 91.0% with relabeling. It does not report or guarantee performance in another setting.
Is the selection a new training plan or a settled choice among these approaches?

It is a choice: adopt overlap-masked reversal contrast. The decision identifies the reversal-detection comparison supporting that choice, but does not provide a separate implementation schedule or claim that any additional deployment step is complete.
